newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Nera sees US$1 bln sales by 2000.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Nera sees US$1 bln sales by 2000.

text.p: Deregulation of the world's telecommunications markets will help Norwegian communications firm Nera ASA boost revenue two and a half times to US$1 billion by 2000, executive chairman Frode Botnevik said on Friday.
Botnevik said Nera, which makes microwave radio-relay systems, antenna and satellite phones for the telecommunications industry, expects half its future revenue to come from Asia.
"For the group as a whole, we forecast that from 1996 to 2000, (revenue) will grow by approximately two and half times to basically US$1 billion," Botnevik told Reuters in an interview.

"With the rapid growth in the Asian economies, hopefully within a couple of years already more than 50 percent of the revenue will come from this region and as we go forward perhaps even more," he added. Nera had a worldwide turnover of 2.63 billion crowns (US$378 million) in 1996, of which 39 percent came from Asia.

Botnevik said the company's growth in Asia and elsewhere was being driven mainly by liberalisation of telecommunications markets which was forcing existing players and new competitors to install new networks with high quality, high speed equipment.
Many of the new networks used microwave systems because they were efficient and allowed companies to recoup their investment faster than conventional land-based systems, he said.

"With deregulation and privatisation today there is a lot of private money going into the telecommunications sector and private money typically is seeking faster returns than the old state telephone companies," he said.
"The largest slice of the pie is the transmission segment, or microwave systems," he said.

"The fastest way to be in business is to install a microwave network instead of going down and digging ditches and laying cables and discussing with landlords rights of way. We build the whole infrastructure, antenna, equipment, everything."

"With digital technology, you can take 2,000 phone calls in one signal through the air and you can combine five or six of these systems. You can start by installing one system and as your customer base grows you can add on," he said.
The managing director of Nera's Southeast Asian unit, Samuel Ang, said he saw the privatisation of Asian telecommunications as an opportunity for huge expansion.

"What we've seen with liberalisation is that existing operators have to upgrade their networks and also have to add microwave systems," Ang said. "The competition is coming out with much better systems so they have to upgrade."

Botnevik agreed: "That is really what is driving the business. That's what we've seen when deregulation started in Thailand and gradually will see in Malaysia, Singapore, in the Philippines, Indonesia and also eventually in Vietnam."
Nera has received approval in principle to list its shares on the main board of the Stock Exchange of Singapore.
The company already has a primary listing on the Oslo bourse and a secondary listing on NASDAQ in New York but wants the Singapore listing to increase its Asian exposure, Botnevik said.

"The main reason for the listing is really to expand our business profile in Asia," he said. "So the listing is not really for the cash. But since we are doing a listing we feel it is also right to issue some new shares to make some liquidity available for the local market."
Nera expects to list in Singapore in May but has yet to release details of the offering.
